title: Silver Trumpets and the First March from Sinai
summary: God orders two silver trumpets to call the people together and signal the camps to move, and to be blown in battle and at festivals as a reminder before him. Then, on the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, the cloud lifts and Israel sets out from Sinai in the order God had laid down. Moses urges his Midianite in-law Hobab to come along as a guide, and the ark goes ahead of the people while Moses calls on the LORD to rise up and to return.
story: This is the hinge of the book. For nearly a year, since arriving at Sinai in the third month after the exodus (Exodus 19:1), Israel has been receiving the law, building the tabernacle, and, in Numbers 1 to 9, being counted, arranged, cleansed, and prepared. Now the preparations end and the march begins. Everything the reader has learned about the camp is set in motion: Judah leads, the Levites carry the tabernacle in two groups, Dan guards the rear. For a few verses, the ordered people God designed actually moves as he intended. The next chapter will show how quickly that order meets complaint, but this chapter lets the reader see the plan working first, and it ends with a prayer that God himself would go before them.
historical:
The departure is precisely dated to the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, nineteen days after the census began (1:1). The destination given is the Wilderness of Paran, a broad desert region generally placed in the northeastern Sinai peninsula, south of Canaan. Trumpets were used in the ancient world for signals in war and worship. Two trumpets were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun, one of silver and one of bronze or copper, from Egypt in the fourteenth century BC. The relief on the Arch of Titus in Rome, showing spoils carried from the Jerusalem temple in AD 70, includes a pair of long trumpets beside the table and lampstand.

Hobab's identity raises a known puzzle. Moses' father-in-law is called Reuel in Exodus 2:18 and Jethro in Exodus 3:1, and here Hobab is Reuel's son, while Judges 4:11 calls Hobab the father-in-law of Moses. The Hebrew word used can mean a relative by marriage more broadly, so many take Hobab to be Moses' brother-in-law. Others think Reuel may be a clan name, or that the traditions come from different sources. The text does not say whether Hobab agreed, but Judges 1:16 records the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite, settling with the tribe of Judah, which suggests that he or his family did come.
cultural:
These trumpets, hammered from silver, were straight metal instruments, distinct from the shofar, the curved ram's horn used elsewhere in the Bible. The signals were simple and practical: both trumpets for the whole congregation, one for the leaders, short blasts to break camp in order, long blasts to assemble. Only the priests blew them, which meant that the call to move always came from the sanctuary. In battle and at festivals the trumpets did something more: they served so that Israel would be “remembered before the LORD” (verse 9). In Scripture, when God remembers, he acts on behalf of those he remembers.

Moses' plea to Hobab reflects the realities of desert travel. Local nomads knew where to find water and pasture, where a large group could camp, and which routes were passable. Moses offers him a share in the good things the LORD had promised Israel, an invitation to an outsider to join the people and its future.
literary: The chapter has three parts. The trumpet law (verses 1-10) closes the long Sinai section of the book with a permanent statute. The march (verses 11-28) is a narrative told almost entirely as a list, repeating the leaders' names from chapter 2 and filling in what chapter 2 left general: the Gershonites and Merarites march after Judah's camp so that the tabernacle can be set up before the Kohathites arrive with the holy objects. The final part (verses 29-36) slows into a personal conversation and then into poetry. The two short sayings of Moses in verses 35-36 have long been called the Song of the Ark. In the traditional Hebrew text they are set off by special scribal marks, inverted forms of the letter nun, and rabbinic tradition discussed them as a small book of their own. Psalm 68 opens with an echo of verse 35.

outline.t: Two silver trumpets: calls to assemble and to march
The priests' trumpets in battle and at festivals
The cloud lifts and Israel leaves Sinai
Moses invites Hobab to come as a guide
The ark goes ahead: the Song of the Ark

doctrines.note: God leads by the cloud and the ark, yet Moses still asks Hobab to be the people's eyes. The chapter holds God's guidance and human wisdom together; divine direction does not make practical knowledge unnecessary.

The trumpets are a way for Israel to be remembered before God in battle and in worship, and Moses' words over the ark are short prayers for God to go ahead of his people and to dwell among them. Israel's march is framed by prayer at its start and at every stop.

The ark, the throne of the invisible King, goes ahead of the army, and Moses calls on the LORD to rise so that his enemies scatter. Israel's march is presented as the procession of a King whose people follow him.

words.note: Chatsotserah, trumpet. It refers to a straight metal trumpet, here of hammered silver, different from the shofar or ram's horn. In the Old Testament these trumpets are nearly always in the hands of priests and appear at key moments of worship, including the dedication of Solomon's temple and the rebuilding of the temple after the exile.

Teruah, a shout or blast. It can mean a battle cry, a shout of joy, or a trumpet signal, here the short blasts that set the camps in motion. The first day of the seventh month is later called a day for sounding trumpets (29:1), which Jewish tradition calls Yom Teruah and keeps as Rosh Hashanah.

Zakhar, to remember. When the trumpets sound, Israel will “be remembered before the LORD” (verse 9). In the Bible, God's remembering is not recalling a forgotten fact; it is turning to act for someone, as he remembered Noah in the flood and his covenant with Abraham in Egypt.

Menuchah, resting place or rest. The ark goes ahead “to seek a resting place for them” (verse 33). The word becomes important later: Psalm 95:11 has God swearing that the rebellious generation “shall never enter My rest,” and Psalm 132:8 prays for God to rise to his resting place with the ark.

christ: Moses' cry, “Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered,” became the opening of Psalm 68, a psalm that pictures God marching in victory and ascending on high. Paul quotes that psalm of Christ's ascension: “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). The ark going before Israel “to seek a resting place for them” also fits a larger biblical thread. The wilderness generation never entered that rest (Psalm 95:11), and Hebrews concludes, “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), found by trusting Christ. Jesus himself said, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Even the trumpets have a future in the New Testament, which speaks of Christ's return “with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). These are the New Testament's own uses of the chapter's images; they fulfill patterns rather than predictions.

hard.q: If God was guiding Israel by the cloud, why did Moses need Hobab to guide them?
hard.a: Some interpreters see Moses' request as a small failure of trust, a leader reaching for a human guide when God had promised to lead, and they note that the next verses stress that the ark and the cloud went ahead. Others see no conflict at all. The cloud determined when Israel moved and where it stopped overall, but a people of this size still needed someone who knew the terrain, the water sources, and the local tribes along the way. On this view, God's guidance works through ordinary knowledge rather than replacing it, and Moses' invitation also brings an outsider into the blessings promised to Israel. The text itself does not criticize Moses, and it leaves Hobab's answer unrecorded, moving straight to the ark leading the way. Readers who take either view agree that the final word belongs to God's presence going ahead.

questions: The trumpets meant Israel would be remembered before God in battle and in celebration. How does prayer in both hard and joyful times shape your sense of being remembered by God?
Moses wanted Hobab's practical knowledge even with the cloud overhead. Where do you tend to set God's guidance and ordinary wisdom against each other?
Moses prayed every time the ark moved and every time it stopped. What would it look like to begin and end the transitions of your life with prayer?
